title: Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
description: Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say
body: Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say.The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire.Romanian President Nicușor Dan confirmed that the Wine Trader and another chemical tanker in the area, the Yara J, had both been struck by drones - the Yara J on Wednesday.  The Wine Trader was empty of cargo at the time.Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port had been hit. It did not name the vessels.Overnight, a swarm of Russian drones was detected not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island.The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.A search and rescue operation for the missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel.The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.The Wine Trader tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 (05:00 GMT).Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader had been hit by two drones.The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked. This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened.The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state."Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region.The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area.Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine.A fire broke out on the Comoros-flagged Yara J late on Wednesday after being struck by a drone, but its crew - who are all reportedly safe - were able to douse the flames themselves.Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports. Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

schema.headline: Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast

title: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia over her legal credentials
description: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.President Donald Trump describe
body: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week. She has referred to herself as a lawyer. But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China." She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.It is seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US. The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself. She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.The new press secretary also told the paper that when she answered China to a question about her bar exam, it was a misunderstanding. She had mistakenly thought, above the din of Marine One, the reporter had asked: "Where were you after law school?"Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment, as well as Zhong Lun Law Firm.It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work. Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

schema.headline: White House defends new press secretary Katie Zacharia over her legal credentials

title: Imran Khan: Bollywood actor asked to leave India after participating in CJP protest in Mumbai
description: Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a
body: Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms.An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections."Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday.Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court.Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting.But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest.The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic".Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na.He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992.Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly.The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade.On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges."Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement.The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India". Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest. "I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said.He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation.Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters. He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform.Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call. On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi.On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital.

schema.headline: Imran Khan: Bollywood actor asked to leave India after participating in CJP protest in Mumbai

title: Albania protests: Student protesters attack government ministries in Tirana
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on WednesdayByRachel FlynnThousands of students have taken to the streets i
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on WednesdayByRachel FlynnThousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects. Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gatesRiot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them. One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania". "The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said. Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".  Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters."Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said. Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters. "The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Central Tirana on Wednesday evening

schema.headline: Albania protests: Student protesters attack government ministries in Tirana

title: Nepal floods: Why Balendra Shah wants India and China to work together in the Himalayan region
description: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disast
body: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions."Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage."The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.And the dangers extend beyond flooding. A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort."One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute."What happened after that no one knows," he added.Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes."These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group.But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved.One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value."What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank.Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders.The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow."There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD.He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks.Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay."Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says.Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

schema.headline: Nepal floods: Why Balendra Shah wants India and China to work together in the Himalayan region

title: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms
description: A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings wit
body: A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country."This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast," the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it. "I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC. A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernautA new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators. Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.  There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand. "This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US senator working on data centre legislation."There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the pushback against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago."People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran war and various aspects of the economy.Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.Yet, recent research, external from the Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centre project.Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees. Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials. Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres."This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle," the NRSC added.  Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed. Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".It could play a part in the state's upcoming Senate race too.Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand."There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project. "She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

schema.headline: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms

title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the USBySam FenwickH
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the USBySam FenwickHost – Follow the Money: Business DailyOn the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , externalLast year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , externalWith Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.The factoryGuangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.Image source, MihoxImage caption, The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 peopleSo, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.Image source, MihoxImage caption, Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail priceAverage pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report, external at the start of this year.Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.The shipFrom the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.The US borderOnce the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China."We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.The US toy companyImage source, Basic FunImage caption, Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the countryThe cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys."It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

schema.headline: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?

title: Why is Starlink internet so important in the Ukraine war?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Starlink terminals, which connect to thousands of SpaceX satellites in obit, are often camouflaged on the
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Starlink terminals, which connect to thousands of SpaceX satellites in obit, are often camouflaged on the battlefieldByTom McArthur and Tiffany WertheimerUpdated 4 hours agoStarlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless. "Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Operators use the Starlink network to stay connected to weapons like drones, so they can see targets in real timeWhat are Starlink and Starshield?Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields. It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade sister service, designed for the Pentagon. Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.How does Starlink work on a battlefield?Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".This makes them ideal for use on the battlefield."It's a connection… that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme."It simplifies our work because we can translate or stream our reconnaissance operations," he added.The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time, effectively minimising the time between "sensor-to shooter", Barros told the BBC.Because Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.When it comes to Ukraine's self-defence, it relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros added.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning the Starlink restriction made Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.For Neo, this means that any deliberate restrictions on the Starlink network are "a betrayal".With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.Image source, Lev Radin/ Getty ImagesImage caption, Starlink terminals, like this one in Ukraine's Donetsk region, are quick and easy to set up, making them ideal for use on the battlefieldWhile Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it.Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine."If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024.But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not.Why did Starlink restrict drone speeds?The answer remains unclear. During a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky had said he hoped it was just a mistake, however, in a later interview with the Financial Times, he said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will."Musk said that Starshield is managed by the US government and suggested the Pentagon could be responsible."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X, external. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the president of the United States]."He added: "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."The BBC has contacted the White House and Pentagon for comment.Image source, EPAImage caption, A Ukrainian soldier attaches a Starlink transmitter to a 'Vampire' attack drone in the  Donetsk region, eastern Ukraine, in JuneThe restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that left 600,000 without power and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.Relations between the US and Ukraine have worsened recently, especially since the US announced a deal with Russia to import its diesel into the American market.Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and in response Donald Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".On Sunday, Trump announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, but three days later, Ukraine said it would resume the strikes, accusing Russia of ignoring it (the Kremlin said it had never agreed to a ceasefire), and the US of withdrawing crucial support.Zelensky has accused the US of threatening to withhold intelligence if Ukraine continues striking Russian oil facilities. Trump has denied this, but last week told reporters that Zelensky had "better damn well stop" the strikes.While in London, Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US.Trump's deal with Russia is his administration's latest effort to lower US fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which started in February, has seen prices skyrocket, souring his standing with the American public.

schema.headline: Why is Starlink internet so important in the Ukraine war?

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
description: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previo
body: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die"."I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.  The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.

schema.headline: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad

title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
description: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery after Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.Ukra
body: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery after Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.Ukraine's president said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and he said curbs on Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.Ukrainian defence sources told the BBC some Starlink functionality had resumed as of Thursday morning.They said its military service Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, although it remains unclear whether the restrictions to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake"."Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."He added: "Peace will be achieved when [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.The Ukrainian president told the FT he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

schema.headline: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume

title: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses
description: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital
body: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".Warning: This article contains distressing detailsAn English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said."I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away.""There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak. Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.

schema.headline: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses

title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
description: Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week
body: Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it. The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote. Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it." The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers."It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media. Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life. The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores."My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil."I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."

schema.headline: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula

title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
description: A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours. China i
body: A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours. China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties.The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC."Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds."China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.   But the alliance is not without tension.Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan. China's attitude has shifted more recently. "Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war. At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops. Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties. Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month. Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un."The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul."But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

schema.headline: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay

title: Barack Obama tells Glasgow audience drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
description: Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope
body: Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hopeBut he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill"."It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said."So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler. "We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'.""We have not chosen to do that."Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet." He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible."I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted."We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.

schema.headline: Barack Obama tells Glasgow audience drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'

title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings without public outcome, BBC Verify finds
description: ByMerlyn ThomasBBC Verify correspondent and Maryam AhmedBBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of kill
body: ByMerlyn ThomasBBC Verify correspondent and Maryam AhmedBBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.How does the IDF investigate incidents?The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers.A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations.In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations.In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation.The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents", external, had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war.These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked.Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security".It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures".The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own"."That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments."[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".GazaSince the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.Image source, Latin Patriarchate of JerusalemImage caption, Nahida and Samar Anton were killed by Israeli troops in Gaza in December 2023BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church".
